title: THE PERSISTENT CHALLENGE OF SMALL-SCALE MINING
text: THE PERSISTENT CHALLENGE OF SMALL-SCALE MININGPOLITICSDear Osagyefo, I'm writing to you again about the devastating impact of small-scale surface mining or galamsey, on our water bodies. Despite numerous attempts to curb this menace, including deploying a "heart surgeon" to the forest, the situation has only worsened. Even the water guards those men and women in Adidas tracks commissioned to tackle galamsey have mysteriously gone missing. Now, Dr. Hannah Bissiw, a seemingly gentle lady, has ventured into the heart of the forest, "Rambo-style," to confront the issue. This move baffles me, especially considering we've previously deployed the military to the same areas with limited success. Yet, Dr. Bissiw, equipped with her own gear, a cameraman and a few policemen somehow successfully arrested several Chinese nationals actively destroying our water bodies. It's ironic, given that this government, when in opposition, vowed to end galamsey within a week, even promising to repeal the Legislative Instrument to ban galamsey in forest preserves. The last time the Deputy Communication Minister was questioned about declaring a state of emergency on galamsey, she skirted the issue, offering a convoluted and evasive response. Compounding this, I've heard the Chinese Ambassador question how his citizens gained access to Ghana's forests, seemingly implying complicity from within our own ranks. Given their skilled labor force, it's not surprising the Chinese are involved in these activities. However, the barbaric treatment Dr. Bissiw allegedly meted out to some individuals, seeing denying even a basic request for water, is deeply concerning and strikes at the core of human dignity. This incident brings to mind the Hawthorne effect: when cameras are rolling, people tend to act differently in her case acting like she's tougher than a brick. Dr. Bissiw's intentions were noble, no doubt, but her "jeans and a dream" approach to galamsey feels a bit like bringing a butter knife to a chainsaw fight. Without a state of emergency or the LI being repealed, her forest trek is sadly destined to be nothing more than a strenuous nature walk with an educational detour to the local kindergarten. Talk is cheap, Ato_kD

filename: A NATIONS DRS DRAMAS AND DELUSIONS.pdf
title: A NATIONS DRS DRAMAS AND DELUSIONS
text:
A NATIONS DRS DRAMAS AND DELUSIONSPOLITICSDear Osagyefo , As we tiptoe into 2026, the Republic is humming with a bizarre blend of football ecstasy and economic heartbreak. Yes, Ghana qualified for the World Cup in the USA, Canada, and Mexico but the joy evaporated faster than the Cedi on a Monday morning. FIFA, in its boundless “kindness,” expanded the tournament by 16 teams, then immediately balanced that generosity by pricing tickets as though they were selling seats on a private shuttle to Jupiter. Ghanaians are now engaged in a nationwide brainstorming session on how to cross the Atlantic, with some wondering whether selling a kidney qualifies as a “strategic financial instrument.” At this point, even the black market is asking us to calm down. While we were busy calculating airfare with the precision of a WAEC examiner marking scripts at midnight, the world was jolted by the dramatic “importation” of Venezuela’s President Maduro, his wife, and their Attorney General to the United States. Before anyone could even whisper “geopolitics,” our very own Honorable Ablakwa sprinted to the global stage with an “open statement” on Ghana’s position. Osagyefo, the letter was so limp it could have doubled as a bookmark in a children’s storybook. There is real danger in poking our noses into high-voltage American legal matters; one misplaced syllable and the US might simply announce, “No visas for Ghanaians,” and that will be the end of our Miami pilgrimage. Someone needs to gently remind the young man of the immortal words of the late Prof. Mills during the Gbagbo saga: Di wo fie asem. We are trying to go and watch football, not audition for a role in a Latin American coup documentary. But if you thought that was the comedic peak, allow me to introduce Dr. Stephen Amoah. A man with a PhD in Actuarial Science a credential he wears like a bulletproof vest in a neighbourhood where no one is shooting. In his attempt to support his preferred candidate in the NPP primary, he delivered a monologue so chaotic it could qualify as experimental theatre. He proudly declared that he is one of only five people on Earth who have cracked a mysterious financial-economic model from 1964. A model so complex that even the global experts who never asked about it are still baffled. Truly, the world is ungrateful.This is the same Dr. Amoah who, in 2019, faced questions about procurement breaches involving 1.1 million cedis paid to an audit firm to investigate whether his predecessor had misused 2 million cedis. In essence, he spent 1 million to find 2 million a financial strategy so innovative it deserves its own TED Talk. When the court asked if he should be held responsible, he delivered a “Yes and No” answer that plunged the room into philosophical crisis. His economic model seems to explain everything except how to give a straight answer or survive a media interview without turbulence.When confronted with the tape, Dr. Amoah claimed “doctoring,” while performing some surgical-grade wordplay of his own. For a man who usually has an answer for everything, he suddenly seemed very busy tiptoeing around the facts. It was less an explanation and more a linguistic interpretive dance the kind that makes judges 
stare into the distance and reconsider their career choices.A man of such rare brilliance should not be lobbying to be a minister in a country of barely 30 million people. He should be in Washington, marching straight into the IMF headquarters to demand his rightful position as Managing Director. After all, why settle for Ghana’s budget when you can supervise the entire planet’s?And in a twist that surprised absolutely no one, word has reached us that the former Finance Minister has been “scouted” by ICE agents in America. It appears my suspicion was correct: the gentleman’s travel plans were strictly one-way. And honestly, can we blame him for preferring an American holding cell over a Ghanaian greeting party? After witnessing Chairman Wontumi lose 50 pounds in a record-breaking 24-hour security-service fitness retreat, the Minister clearly decided he wasn’t ready for that kind of “body transformation.” So long, Ato KD

title: Dear Osagyefo,
text: Dear Osagyefo,I write to you not just as a concerned professional, but as a deeply disturbed consumer of baffling toxicology reports. I was briefly in Ghana, and my curiosity about the "active ingredients" in our local drinks grew, shall we say, dangerously high.You see, I spend my days working with young men who are, for want of a better word, "hooked." When I secured a gig with a non-profit, my first mission was simple: test our famed local beverages. Some of these drinks, marketed as mere food supplements, are lauded for "doing wonders." I now know exactly what wonders they're doing. This whole enterprise began when a frantic gentleman called me last year. Despite his personal assurance that he was completely clean, he had failed a pre-employment urine toxicological screening. The only thing he could recall? Trying some local "herbs" in Ghana for his back pain. He remembered great sleep and morning energy, a clear indication that it was working!We ran our own kit, and the results were a cocktail of controlled chaos: amphetamine, PCP, THC, and benzodiazepine. It appears his back pain remedy was less "herbal tea" and more "pharmacy in a bottle."Just yesterday, I tested samples of two popular sachets: Mandingo and Herb Afrik. The results were not just positive; they were positively terrifying. Herb Afrik contained benzodiazepine, PCP, and MDMA, a relaxing, party-drug mix , all in one convenient pouch! Mandingo contained PCPOne wonders no longer why the youth "get a buzz." They aren't getting a buzz; they are being chemically manipulated with a terrifying medley of street drugs. At this point, I have to question the entire operation: What, precisely, is GIHOC Distilleries distilling, and what, for the love of public health, is the FDA doing? If the FDA is in cohoot with manufacturers who are effectively deceiving Ghanaians with these high-proof, high-drug concoctions, then you might be right. It's a stark piece of irony: the same GIHOC whose drinks are allegedly laced with illicit drugs is dedicating space on their website to a breast cancer campaign. It's about time we put all these local drinks to a test, Alomo next ?? Alarmed,Ato KD

title: Letter XX
text: Letter XXSPEECHES ARE PAPER, CHANGE IS CONCRETE !POLITICSDear Osagyefo,Your last presence at the United Nations General Assembly in 1961 remains a touchstone of African leadership. This year, the current President of the Republic stood on the same global stage in New York, albeit dressed in a colorful smock, to deliver his address to the world.During your time, following the assassination of Patrice Lumumba after his appeal to the UN, you articulated the profound hope that the United Nations represented for world peace. Similarly, President Mahama delivered a powerful address, demanding greater representation for Africa within the UN Security Council structure and highlighting the fundamental injustices that contravene the organization's founding principles.However, the history of this great hall is filled with beautiful speeches that earned standing ovations, from Madiba to the Otumfuo's keynote address six years ago, and, of course, Barack Obama. Again, history tells us anything, it’s that the UN stage is a hall of beautiful, perishable rhetoric. These examples underscore a crucial truth: Words are fleeting and easily forgotten. People are ultimately remembered not by the eloquence of their speeches, but by the tangible changes they effect for humanity. Speeches are paper, change is concrete !Here at home, President Mahama proved he knows the Constitution of Ghana inside and out, using its delicate clauses to expertly arrange the departure of a Chief Justice. Yet, shortly thereafter, he took to the UN General Assembly to champion a cause that seemed to forget the very nature of established power. He was there, passionately demanding reform and railing against the veto power enshrined in Article 27 of the UN Charter that beautiful little rule that lets any P5 member block a substantive resolution and ensures nothing truly binding happens against their core interests.President Mahama once vowed to decisively tackle the destructive illegal mining known as "galamsey." Regrettably, his administration's approach has been arguably the worst in Ghana's history. It appears the fight against this menace has been abandoned, choosing instead to focus on benefiting from the gold proceeds rather than ending the practice that is destroying our water bodies like never before.The landmark repeal of the criminal libel law under Kufuor is being aggressively undermined currently. Politicians, it seems, haven't learned the lessons of history and are rushing to embrace mechanisms that will ultimately silence them. The chilling warning holds true: "Freedom after the speech won't be guaranteed." All those beautiful speeches are wonderful, but you can't clean up a river with a standing ovation. Back home, your water is being destroyed like never before.So much to do, so little done, Ato_KD

filename: ANKWANOMA OSP: THE SINGING PROSECUTOR AND THE BAILED-OUT LAWYER.pdf
title: ANKWANOMA OSP: THE SINGING PROSECUTOR AND THE BAILED-OUT LAWYER
text:
ANKWANOMA OSP: THE SINGING PROSECUTOR AND THE BAILED-OUT LAWYERPOLITICSDear Osagyefo, You’ll be amused to know that the theater of the absurd in our Republic has a new leading man: Martin Kpebu. It appears the man who once championed the cause of the downtrodden is now on a singular mission to perform a final magic trick, trying to make the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) disappear entirely. I remember when Martin first came onto the scene through Joy Newsfile. Back then, he was a very unassuming, learned lawyer, a shy gentleman who seemed to know the Constitution like the palm of his hand. He spoke with the quiet precision of a surgeon. But oh, how times change! The moment he started wearing "The Hat," the transformation was complete. The shy gentleman vanished, replaced by a legal warrior who started throwing missiles at anyone within range. It seems the more prominent the hat, the more explosive the rhetoric. For years, this new, missile-launching Martin stood on a legal high horse, making a mockery of those unfortunate souls caught in the OSP’s net who couldn’t afford their bail. He famously declared with the confidence of a man who sleeps with a law ledger under his pillow—that as a "senior lawyer," it was practically impossible for him to be detained.The irony reached its peak when he, a prominent member of ORAL , the team championing the prosecution and arrest of those who allegedly embezzled state funds , found himself being detained. He who called for the shackles of others suddenly felt the cold steel of the law. This happened after a spirited verbal altercation with security at the OSP office, where insults were reportedly traded like currency. After they "bundled" him away, the OSP office requested a landed property in his name as part of his bail , the ultimate "paperwork" punishment for a man who loves his law books.How else is a lawyer supposed to defend himself if not with his words? Yet, his vocabulary led him straight to a cell. He was then slapped with the very same ridiculous bail conditions that he once ridiculed others for failing to meet. Watching a man who specializes in words being silenced by a demand for a deed was like watching a chef realize he’s allergic to his own dish. While Martin is busy trying to dismantle the office, the Special Prosecutor himself, Kissi Agyebeng, has taken to the airwaves with a surreal defense strategy. He had appeared on TV not just to argue law, but to quote Daddy Lumba’s hit tune "Ankwanoma." He stood there like a lonely bird on a podium, singing about his soul and his "time being up" as if we paid the man to mime on a public stage. If we wanted highlife, we could have hired a band for a fraction of the OSP’s budget, which, by the way, has apparently spent more money than it has actually collected. The comedy is compounded by the political pivot of the NDC MPs. Suddenly, the very people who might have cheered for a strong OSP are calling for its head. It seems that when the "Senior Lawyer" of their liking gets caught in the gears, the whole machine must be scrapped.Martin and his company now claim they possess damning information about the OSP, but he will only share it with the Governing Board. The 
catch? The Board apparently doesn't exist. It’s the perfect legal stalemate: I have the smoking gun, but I’ll only show it to the ghost in the room.So long, Ato KD
